Goal

PLeW is a browser-based visualization tool for multi-dimensional tabular data. Load a dataset, map columns onto grid axes, color, and shape, and inspect or edit individual rows in a record window.

PLeW-NLG is PLeW set up for human evaluation of NLG outputs. Each row is one judgment (one rater's score for one model output on one item), and the record window shows the texts that rating refers to.

This guide walks through: (1) prepare data, (2) load and explore, (3) configure the view, (4) edit annotation values, (5) generate reports, (6) inspect and compare records, (7) save layouts.

We use SimpEval (Maddela et al., 2023) for most steps (600 judgments, five raters, six systems). Other bundled datasets appear only when a feature needs them.

1. Prepare your data

What you need

  1. A flat CSV or JSON file.
  2. One row per judgment (e.g. one rater's score for one output on one item).
  3. A few low-cardinality columns for the grid (system, annotator, score band).
  4. Text or media to show when a dot is clicked.
  5. Roughly 500–2000 rows for smooth use (subset if larger).

Wide tables (one column per rater) must be melted to long format first.

Column prefixes

PrefixRoleExample
dim::Dimension (grid)dim::system, dim::score_band
desc::Text in record windowdesc::original, desc::output
med::Image/audio/videomed::image
res::Reserved metadatares::score (record only, not grid)

Add a stable ID column (first column). See eval-data-processed/simpeval/simpeval_plew_ready.csv for a full example.

Option A: prepare manually

  1. Reshape to one row per judgment.
  2. Prefix columns as dim::, desc::, med::, or res::.
  3. Validate:
python .cursor/skills/plew-prepare-dataset/scripts/validate_plew_csv.py \
  path/to/your_dataset_plew_ready.csv

Option B: use the plew-prepare-dataset skill

  1. Put raw files in eval-data-raw/<dataset>/.
  2. In Cursor, ask: Make eval-data-raw/simpeval/ ready for PLeW.
  3. Check eval-data-processed/<dataset>/ for: <dataset>_plew_ready.csv, PLEW_MANIFEST.md, and transform.py.
  4. To change sampling or mappings, edit transform.py and rerun:
python eval-data-processed/simpeval/transform.py

If the data cannot be converted, the skill writes PLEW_UNSUITABLE.md instead.

2. Run PLeW-NLG

Start the server

  1. Install Hugo Extended (once): brew install hugo (macOS), winget install Hugo.Hugo.Extended (Windows), or a release from github.com/gohugoio/hugo/releases.
  2. From the project root, run:
hugo server
  1. Open http://localhost:1313/ in your browser.

If port 1313 is busy: hugo server --port 1314.

Main window

The editor opens with the sidebar on the left and an empty grid on the right until data is loaded (Figure 1). Press B to show or hide the sidebar.

Load your data

Two entry points:

URLUse when
http://localhost:1313/Upload your own CSV or JSON
http://localhost:1313/examples/Browse bundled datasets

For this guide, open SimpEval at http://localhost:1313/examples/simpeval/.

The page loads simpeval.csv automatically. To use a file you prepared, go to http://localhost:1313/ and drop your *_plew_ready.csv in Data input (Figure 2):

You can also follow View example datasets to open bundled examples without uploading.

After import

Once data loads, the grid fills with dots (one per judgment), as in Figure 3. Dimensions are assigned automatically: the first enabled dimension in the sidebar list gets Grid X, the second gets Grid Y, then Color, Shape, and so on. That default layout is not always what you want.

3. Configure the view

3.1 Annotator × score band

A common first view is annotator × score band: rows are raters, columns are score bands. Each dot is still one judgment; you can see how each annotator uses the scale.

Press B to open the sidebar and expand Dimensions. You can set up this view in two ways:

1. Re-order dimensions.

  1. Uncheck dimensions you do not need (e.g. system, sentence_id).
  2. Drag the remaining rows so score_band is first and annotator_index is second.
  3. PLeW updates the dropdowns automatically: the first enabled row becomes Grid X, the second Grid Y, then Color, Shape, and so on.

2. Assign encodings manually.

  1. Uncheck dimensions you do not need (e.g. system, sentence_id).
  2. Leave the list order unchanged.
  3. Open the dropdown on each row and pick an encoding: set score_band to Grid X and annotator_index to Grid Y. Use — to leave a dimension out of the layout.

Figure 4 shows the sidebar after this setup. Figure 5 shows the resulting grid.

You can also open this view ready-made at http://localhost:1313/examples/simpeval/ by choosing Annotator × score band under Views in the top toolbar.

3.2 Tidy the grid

Figure 5 is readable but uneven: outer grid cells differ in height (compare annotator 5 with annotator 1), and inner panels within cells differ too. Before taking a screenshot, use Display options and Label styling in the grid header (Figure 6a and Figure 6b):

  1. In Display options: tick Unify grid sizes and set Height (px) so all outer cells share the same height.
  2. Tick Unify inner panel and set Height (px) so mini-panels inside each cell match.
  3. Optional: tick Show item counts and Show dimension names to add counts and axis labels to the grid.
  4. In Label styling: adjust Column labels size and Inner panel size, and set Column labels color and Inner panel color (especially for 📷 Light snapshots).

3.3 Screenshot the grid

When the layout looks right, capture it from the grid header (next to Download CSV):

📷 Dark 📷 Light

  1. Click 📷 Dark for a dark-background PNG, or 📷 Light for a white background (better for papers and slides).
  2. The browser downloads grid_snapshot.png of the current grid.

The snapshot includes the grid and its labels, but not the sidebar or toolbar. Figure 7a and Figure 7b show the annotator × score band view after tidying, in dark and light themes.

3.4 Four dimensions: sentence, system, annotator, score band

Okay, now we may want to see, for each sentence and each model, how the five annotators scored it. The simple view from §3.1 cannot show that: it collapses all sentences and systems into one grid. Here we keep sentences as rows, models as columns, annotators inside each cell, and score band as color.

We start with a few sentences (11, 12, 19) and map four dimensions:

DimensionEncoding
sentence_idGrid Y (rows)
systemGrid X (columns)
annotator_indexPanel X (x-axis inside each cell)
score_bandColor

Each cell is one (sentence, system) pair. The five dots inside show annotators 1–5; color is the score band each chose.

  1. Press B and expand Dimensions. Check all four dimensions.
  2. Assign encodings manually: sentence_id → Grid Y, system → Grid X, annotator_index → Panel X, score_band → Color.
  3. Filter values so the grid stays readable (see below).

Filtering values

Once dimensions are assigned, the sidebar shows Filter values and Color Legend. Each block lists the values for one dimension. Use the checkboxes to include or exclude values; only checked values appear in the grid.

All selects every value in that list. None clears every checkbox (nothing shown until you tick values again). A typical workflow: click None, then check only the values you want.

In the Color Legend, the default colors for 0–20 and 61–80 are both greenish and hard to tell apart in a dense grid. Click a swatch to open the color picker and assign a clearer color (Figure 9).

Above the grid, the toolbar shows the same color mapping (Figure 10). Tick Show color & shape to display this legend bar (and shape keys when shape is used). Tick Cluster by color to group dots by color within each cell instead of overlapping them. These options are included when you Export setup.

In Figure 11, sentence 19 under lstm_w_split shows five blue dots (all annotators, same score band). Under scramble_words, colors differ (annotators disagree). Use Display options, Label styling, and the snapshot buttons as before.

4. Edit annotation values

PLeW is an editor, not only a viewer. Edits stay in the browser until you download a new CSV. Use the four-dimensional view from the previous section and zoom in on one cell, for example sentence 11 and SEMoses_all (Figure 12).

Scenario 1: raters 2 and 4 were swapped

You discover that the judgments for raters 2 and 4 were recorded under the wrong annotator index. Drag the dot at position 2 to position 4, then drag the dot at position 4 to position 2. Each drag updates dim::annotator_index for that row.

Scenario 2: rater 1 chose the wrong score band

Rater 1 tells you they meant a score in the 41–60 band but the dot shows a higher band (61–80). Right-click the dot at position 1 and pick 41–60 from the color menu. This updates dim::score_band for that judgment.

Figure 13 shows the cell after both fixes. Modified dots are marked on the grid; the sidebar reports how many changes you have made.

Undo, reset, download, and change log

After the first edit, the sidebar shows edit controls and a Change Log (Figure 14):

ControlWhat it does
Undo (Ctrl+Z)Revert the last edit.
Reset AllDiscard every edit and restore the uploaded data.
Download CSVSave the current table, including your edits, with column prefixes preserved.
Change LogList every edit (row, field, old value, new value, time). Export as CSV or JSON, or clear the list.

5. Report

Click Report in the grid header (📋 Report). Reporting is basic for now: it summarizes the currently loaded data (including any edits) as HTML you can download.

  1. Choose Overview (total row count and dimension names).
  2. For each dimension, tick Counts and/or % for value distributions.
  3. Optionally add crosstabs: pick two dimensions (e.g. annotator_index × score_band).
  4. Click Generate, then Download HTML for a standalone summary page.

The example below (open in new tab) was exported from SimpEval. It includes:

  • Overview: 600 rows; dimensions sentence_id, system, annotator_index, score_band.
  • score_band counts and percentages (e.g. 236 rows in 81–100, 39.3%).
  • Crosstab annotator_index × score_band (counts per rater and band).

6. Record windows

PLeW is not only for grid overviews: you can inspect individual judgments and read the text behind each rating. That is often the best way to get a feel for your data. Here we ask a concrete question: for rater 5, how do scores and simplifications differ across the six systems? We reuse the sentence × system layout from §3.4, filter to annotator 5, and open record windows to compare models.

6.1 One annotator per cell

Map four dimensions, then filter annotators:

DimensionEncoding
sentence_idGrid Y
systemGrid X
score_bandColor
annotator_indexShape
  1. Press B and expand Dimensions. Enable sentence_id, system, score_band, and annotator_index.
  2. Assign sentence_id → Grid Y, system → Grid X, score_band → Color, annotator_index → Shape.
  3. Under Filter values, restrict sentence_id to 11, 12, and 19 as before.
  4. For annotator_index, click None, then check only 5.

Each cell now shows one dot: annotator 5's rating for that sentence and system. Color is the score band; shape is the annotator (Figure 16).

6.2 Open a record

Click any dot to open the record window for that judgment. The default layout lists every column, often in an order that is hard to scan when you mainly want to compare original text and simplification (Figure 17).

6.3 Customize column roles

The default record window (Figure 17) lists every column, often with dimensions first. That order is awkward when you mainly want to read the original and the simplification. You may also want a more minimal window: for instance, limit it to the ID, the original and simplification text, the scores, and the system that produced it, and hide everything else from the record window.

In the sidebar, open Column roles (Figure 18). Each row is one field. You can:

  • Drag the handle to reorder fields in the record window.
  • Click the eye icon to show or hide a field in the record window (hidden fields stay in the dataset).

For this example, put the fields in reading order and hide the rest:

  1. Drag to: ID, original, simplification, system, score, score_band.
  2. Turn off the eye for fields you do not need in the window, e.g. annotator_index, sentence_id, and generation_raw.

Open the same record again (Figure 20): ID at the top, original and simplification together, then system, score, and score band.

6.4 Compare records

With the grid from §6.1, you can compare two judgments side by side. For example, on sentence 12, rater 5 gave 95 to asset.test.simp but 20 to SEMoses_all. You want to read both simplifications next to each other.

  1. Click the dot for the higher-rated output (e.g. asset.test.simp on sentence 12). It opens in slot A.
  2. Shift+click the dot for the lower-rated output (e.g. SEMoses_all on the same sentence). It loads in slot B.

The window switches to Compare records: one column per slot, one row per field (Figure 21). The slot bar shows which records are selected. Use Clear B or Clear all to reset.

To export the comparison, use 📷 Dark or 📷 Light in the record window header — the same snapshot buttons as the main grid. The snapshot includes the comparison table only, not the grid behind it.

The full layout for this section (grid encodings, filters, display options, and column roles) is saved in plew-setup-simpeval_plew_ready_record_windows.json. Load SimpEval, then use Import setup (§7) to restore the view from Figures 16–21 without repeating the steps above.

As in Figure 18, each field in Column roles also has a role dropdown (Dimension, Description, Reserved metadata). After import, you may find a column was tagged wrong: for example, you want a field on the grid as a dimension rather than as description text in the record window, or the other way around. Change the role in Column roles and PLeW updates the sidebar and grid immediately. You do not need to edit the CSV prefixes and reload.

7. Reproducibility

To build a view like Figure 11, you made many choices: which dimensions map to Grid X, Grid Y, Color, and Panel X; which sentences and score bands to filter; custom colors; display and label settings. That is a reproducibility risk: you may not recreate the same layout weeks later, and colleagues who load the CSV alone will not see your view unless you document every step.

PLeW stores the full layout in a JSON setup file. Export it and share it with the dataset so others can restore the exact view.

  1. Press B to open the sidebar and expand Visualization setup (Figure 22).
  2. Click Export setup to download a JSON file (dimension order, encodings, filters, custom colors, display options, and more).
  3. To restore the view later, load the same CSV and click Import setup, then select that JSON file.

Share the PLeW-ready CSV (or a link to the example page) together with the setup JSON. Anyone with both files can import the JSON and get the same grid, filters, and colors without repeating the manual steps in this guide.

Named presets on example pages

The bundled SimpEval views (Annotator × score band, and so on) are the same JSON files, saved under static/data/ and wired into the example page. You can add your own:

  1. Configure the view, then Export setup from the sidebar.
  2. Save the file in static/data/, e.g. plew-setup-my-view.json.
  3. In the example page front matter (e.g. content/examples/simpeval.md), add:
[[viz_presets]]
label = "My view name"
url = "data/plew-setup-my-view.json"

Restart hugo server if needed. The new name appears under Views in the top toolbar; clicking it applies the saved layout. Share the CSV, the JSON file, and (for a permanent gallery entry) the front-matter snippet so others can reproduce or host the same preset.
